blocks.text: Kidney disease is often **silent early on**. Many patients are picked up through raised blood pressure, an abnormal dipstick or routine blood tests, not symptoms. When symptoms are present they fall into four groups: a **change in how the urine looks**, **disturbed micturition**, **loin or suprapubic pain**, and **systemic (uraemic) symptoms** of kidney failure.

blocks.title: Urine volume terms (Davidson definitions)
rows: About 650 mL/day is the least that still clears the daily solute load
Strong pointer to a **sudden** kidney injury (e.g. pre-renal AKI)
Complete obstruction, bilateral loss of renal perfusion, or RPGN
High intake, osmotic diuresis (glucose, calcium), cranial or nephrogenic DI, loss of concentrating ability in CKD
Polyuria, evening fluid/caffeine/diuretics, CKD, prostatic enlargement, or just poor sleep

blocks.title: Causes of anuria
items: **Complete obstruction:** prostatic retention, bilateral ureteric obstruction (retroperitoneal fibrosis, cancer), bilateral staghorn stones
**Bilateral loss of perfusion:** aortic dissection involving the renal arteries, severe ATN, cardiorenal or hepatorenal states
**Rapidly progressive GN:** anti-GBM disease, severe ANCA vasculitis

blocks.title: Uraemic symptoms to ask about
items: Anorexia, weight loss, metallic taste, nausea and vomiting
Malaise, fatigue, insomnia, hiccups, restless legs
Itch, easy bruising, oedema, bone pain
Nocturia and polyuria; symptoms of anaemia
Amenorrhoea in women; erectile dysfunction in men
Advanced uraemia: slowed thinking, clouded consciousness, myoclonic twitching, seizures
Usually present once urea is above about **40 mmol/L**, though many patients get symptoms at lower levels

blocks.text: **Timing the disease from the history:** oliguria suggests an acute injury. Months or years of **polyuria and nocturia** suggest long-standing CKD, because failing tubules cannot concentrate urine. Also look for old urinalysis or creatinine results (insurance, pre-employment or new-patient checks).

**Anuria thresholds differ between books.** Davidson defines anuria as **< 100 mL/day**; Talley uses < 50 mL/day. Oliguria is < 400 mL/day in both. Use Davidson in the exam. Urine volume alone is a poor guide to severity: GFR can be very low with a normal volume.

sections.title: Haematuria, proteinuria & the colour of urine

blocks.title: Clues in the haematuria history
rows: Repeated episodes over months, often after a URTI
Blood only at the start of the stream, then clear
Blood only at the end of voiding

blocks.text: **Red urine is not always blood.** Rifampicin, large amounts of beetroot, haemoglobinuria and myoglobinuria can all colour the urine; in porphyria it changes colour on standing. A dipstick positive for blood with **no red cells on microscopy** means haemoglobin (intravascular haemolysis) or myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis, brown urine).

blocks.title: Who needs what after haematuria (Davidson)
items: First exclude **menstruation and UTI**
**Visible haematuria** is most often caused by tumour, so refer to urology for ultrasound/CT and cystoscopy
**Persistent non-visible haematuria** (2 of 3 dipsticks) in anyone **over 40** also needs imaging and cystoscopy
Raised BP, low eGFR, raised ACR, a family history of kidney disease or systemic disease: refer to nephrology and consider biopsy
Otherwise: yearly urinalysis, BP, ACR and eGFR

blocks.title: Nephritic vs nephrotic presentation
rows: Red or brown urine, often scanty
Frothy (foamy) urine; swelling, often facial puffiness on waking
Hypertension, oliguria, fluid retention, falling renal function
Low serum albumin, oedema, generalised fluid retention
Post-streptococcal GN, anti-GBM disease, small-vessel vasculitis

blocks.text: **Proteinuria numbers (Davidson):** healthy people excrete **< 150 mg/day**. Dipsticks turn positive at about **0.5 g/24 hrs**. More than **1 g/day** (PCR > 100 mg/mmol, ACR > 70 mg/mmol) makes glomerular disease likely and is an indication for biopsy. Above 3.5 g/day (PCR > 350) is nephrotic range. Test an **early-morning sample** to exclude benign orthostatic proteinuria.

**Books disagree on protein cut-offs.** Kumar gives normal excretion as < 30 mg/day and calls a uPCR > 200 mg/mmol glomerular. Davidson gives < 150 mg/day and treats PCR > 100 mg/mmol (about 1 g/day) as likely glomerular. Both agree a PCR > 350 is nephrotic range. Use Davidson.

blocks.note: Causes of haematuria laid out from kidney to urethra: GN, vasculitis, cysts, tumours, infarction, stones, pyelonephritis, cystitis, bladder tumour, prostate, urethritis, trauma.
Haematuria work-up algorithm: urology referral for visible haematuria or non-visible haematuria over 40; nephrology if BP, eGFR or ACR is abnormal.

sections.title: Pain, lower urinary tract symptoms, UTI & obstruction

blocks.title: Localising urinary tract pain
rows: Loin pain radiating to the groin
Severe colicky or constant loin pain radiating to the symphysis, perineum or testis; nausea; with haematuria this is typical of a stone
Loin pain brought on by a large fluid intake (Dietl's crisis)
Loin or back pain with high fever, vomiting, looking unwell; renal angle tenderness
Rarely painful; at most a dull ache
A frequent cause of loin pain that is not renal at all

blocks.text: Pain that is **worse after a fluid load** (alcohol, coffee, diuretics) suggests **acute obstruction**: high urine flow distends the blocked collecting system.

blocks.title: Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)
rows: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, urge incontinence, nocturia
Bladder irritation: UTI, STI, bladder stones, prostatitis
Hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, straining, terminal dribbling
Repeatedly passing small, painful, bloody volumes
Needing to void again soon after finishing

blocks.title: Types of established incontinence
items: **Stress:** leaks on coughing; women after vaginal delivery or with postmenopausal atrophy
**Urge:** detrusor overactivity
**Detrusor underactivity:** neurological causes
**Overflow:** dribbling from a full bladder, e.g. prostatic obstruction
**Vesico/urethral fistula:** after obstructed labour
Incontinence is **not** part of normal ageing

blocks.title: UTI in the history
items: **Risk factors:** female sex, intercourse, pregnancy, diabetes, catheter, previous UTI, outflow obstruction
**Lower UTI:** dysuria, suprapubic pain, frequency, urgency, incontinence
**Pyelonephritis:** high fever, loin or back pain, vomiting, anorexia, haematuria, looking systemically unwell
**Most useful clues:** a woman's own belief that she has a UTI (LR+ 4.0). Vaginal discharge argues **against** UTI (LR+ 0.3). Dysuria (LR+ 1.5) and haematuria (LR+ 2.0) help less

blocks.text: **Complete anuria** suggests complete bilateral obstruction (or obstruction of a single functioning kidney). **Alternating anuria and polyuria** suggests intermittent complete obstruction. Partial obstruction can cause polyuria.

In the **elderly**, both UTI and acute urinary retention may present with **confusion alone**. Frequent small voids with a tender, palpable bladder suggest **retention with overflow**. Retention from neurological disease (e.g. MS) may be painless.
A UTI in **any man**, or frequent or relapsing UTIs in a woman, suggests an anatomical abnormality and needs urological evaluation.

sections.title: Drug, past & family history; AKI framework; CKD and RRT patients

blocks.title: History clues: pre-renal, renal or post-renal?
rows: Intercurrent illness (especially sepsis), vomiting or diarrhoea, hypotension, ACE inhibitor/ARB or diuretic use, liver failure (hepatorenal), renovascular disease

Disease with renal involvement (e.g. myeloma), nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, contrast), rhabdomyolysis or haemoglobinuria (pigment ATN), PPIs or sulfonamides (interstitial nephritis), systemic inflammatory symptoms, proteinuria
Obstructive urinary symptoms, complete anuria, prostate disease, bladder or pelvic cancer

blocks.title: Drug history
items: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs and diuretics; recent **contrast** (angiography, CT, MRI)
Aminoglycosides, PPIs, lithium (nephrogenic DI)
Ask directly about **over-the-counter** and **herbal/traditional** remedies
Many renally cleared drugs need dose adjustment, so take a full list
Long-term compound analgesic use suggests analgesic nephropathy, which needs surveillance for urothelial cancer

blocks.title: Past and family history
items: **Past:** diabetes, hypertension, earlier proteinuria or haematuria, biopsy-proven GN, recurrent UTI or stones, gout, previous AKI, chemo/radiotherapy, myeloma, blood-borne viruses
**Systemic disease:** rash or arthritis (SLE, scleroderma); fever, eye inflammation, hair thinning, nasal discharge, haemoptysis (vasculitis)
Bed-wetting beyond age 3 suggests vesicoureteric reflux with renal scarring
Vascular disease elsewhere (IHD, stroke) raises suspicion of renovascular disease
**Family:** polycystic kidney disease (autosomal dominant; family history absent in about 20%), diabetes, hypertension, any relative on dialysis
**Deafness plus kidney disease** in the family suggests Alport syndrome
**Social:** coping, work, support, home dialysis arrangements

blocks.title: Patients with CKD, on dialysis or with a transplant
items: **CKD complications:** bone pain and fractures, hypercalcaemia symptoms, pericarditis, heart failure, IHD, neuropathy, peptic ulceration
**Dialysis:** HD or PD and how often; fluid restriction; phosphate binders taken with meals; weight gain between sessions; residual urine output; fistula problems or hypotension; transplant listing
**PD red flag:** abdominal pain with fever means peritonitis until proven otherwise
**Transplant:** graft function, rejection episodes, number of grafts, donor type, missed immunosuppressant doses, infections, skin cancers, steroid hypertension or weight gain
**Advanced CKD:** what they understand, and whether they want RRT or a supportive approach

blocks.title: Acute or chronic? Dating the disease from the history
items: **Oliguria** points to a sudden (acute) kidney injury
Long-standing **nocturia and polyuria** point to CKD: failing tubules lose concentrating ability, and nocturia can be an early symptom
Ask how long any symptoms have been present
Look for **old urinalysis or creatinine results** (insurance or pre-employment medicals, new-patient checks)

blocks.text: CKD means kidney damage or GFR < 60 for **3 months or more**, whatever the cause. In **secondary** hyperparathyroidism calcium is low and phosphate high. In **tertiary** (autonomous) hyperparathyroidism both are high.
Patients often **forget over-the-counter NSAIDs and herbal remedies** unless you ask about them by name, and both often contribute to kidney injury.

The renal examination has four aims: assess **fluid status**, look for signs of **uraemia/CKD**, look for **clues to the cause**, and find evidence of past or current **renal replacement therapy**. Few signs are specific to uraemia.

blocks.title: General inspection, hands and skin
rows: Hiccups, uraemic fetor, sallow or yellow tinge
Scars from old shunts or carpal tunnel surgery
Previous haemodialysis access; dialysis-related carpal tunnel syndrome

blocks.title: Face, neck, chest and legs
rows: Basal cell carcinoma or other skin cancer
Raised JVP, basal crackles, extra heart sounds

blocks.title: Fluid status, blood pressure and fundi
items: Assess fluid balance in **every** renal patient. Depletion can cause AKI or worsen CKD; too much IV fluid can cause pulmonary oedema
**Regular weighing** is the objective measure of fluid status
**Depleted:** dry mouth, reduced skin turgor, postural hypotension
**Overloaded:** raised JVP, basal crackles, oedema, hypoxia with hypertension

Oedema collects at the ankles by day and at the **sacrum** in bed-bound patients. **Facial oedema on waking** is common in nephrotic syndrome. Unilateral oedema suggests DVT, inflammation or lymphatic disease
Always measure **BP** (hypertension is both cause and complication) and test for a **postural drop**
**Fundoscopy** for hypertensive and diabetic retinopathy

blocks.title: Dialysis access (a common exam station)
items: **AV fistula:** look at skin integrity and for aneurysms, feel for a **thrill** over the anastomosis, listen for a **machinery murmur**
Sites: radio-cephalic, brachio-cephalic, or (less often) brachio-basilic. Needs 4 weeks to 4 months to mature
Complications: aneurysm, infection, thrombosis, stenosis, steal syndrome (distal ischaemia), high-output heart failure
**Tunnelled cuffed catheter:** jugular or subclavian entry, tip in SVC/right atrium, two lumens (red out, blue in), Dacron cuff that anchors it and resists infection

blocks.text: **Chronic rather than acute kidney failure** is suggested by small kidneys (except in PKD, diabetes, amyloidosis and myeloma), renal bone disease, normocytic anaemia and peripheral neuropathy.
**Never take blood from an AV fistula** or use that arm casually: the fistula is the patient’s dialysis lifeline.

blocks.note: Physical signs of advanced CKD: yellow complexion, pallor, brown-line nails, scratch marks, bruising, pericardial rub, raised JVP, acidotic breathing; RRT signs such as a fistula, dialysis line and Tenckhoff catheter.
Mees' lines: a single transverse white band across the nails.
Forearm AV fistula: a long swelling with a continuous thrill.

blocks.title: Abdominal inspection
items: **Tenckhoff catheter**, or small lower-midline scars from old PD catheters
**Nephrectomy scars** are often posterior, so roll the patient and look at the loins
**Transplant scar** in the right or left iliac fossa, often with a bulge from the superficial graft
Distension from **polycystic kidneys** or ascites
Scrotal masses and genital oedema

blocks.title: Palpation and percussion
items: An enlarged kidney bulges **forwards**; perinephric collections bulge **backwards**
**Ballotting:** one hand under the renal angle flicks upwards while the other, on the upper quadrant, feels the kidney rise and fall
Transplanted kidneys lie superficially and are easy to feel. **Tenderness over a graft** may mean rejection
Feel for an enlarged **bladder** and an **aortic aneurysm**
In abdominal pain, **loin tenderness** strongly supports renal colic (LR+ 27.7)
**Auscultatory percussion of the bladder:** an upper border < 2 cm above the stethoscope means a near-empty bladder; > 8 cm means about 750 mL–1 L

blocks.title: Causes of palpable kidneys
rows: Normal right kidney or solitary kidney
Compensatory hypertrophy of a single kidney
Acute renal vein thrombosis, pyelonephritis, renal abscess

blocks.title: If you find polycystic kidneys
items: Measure **BP**: about 75% are hypertensive
Dipstick for haematuria and proteinuria (usually < 2 g/day)
Look for anaemia, or polycythaemia from high erythropoietin
Hepatomegaly or splenomegaly from cysts; a tender kidney may be an infected cyst
Associations: subarachnoid haemorrhage (3%), mitral regurgitation
Autosomal dominant, so assess family members

blocks.title: Auscultation, back and pelvis
items: **Renal bruits:** listen about 2 cm either side of the midline above the umbilicus, then in both flanks
About **50%** of renal artery stenosis has a bruit. A **systolic-diastolic** bruit in hard-to-control hypertension has LR+ > 40; a soft systolic bruit alone is often insignificant
**Flash pulmonary oedema** in a hypertensive patient with renal impairment makes renal artery stenosis more likely; normal BP makes it less likely
**Back:** spinal tenderness (renal osteodystrophy, myeloma). Back pain with renal failure should raise suspicion of a **paraprotein**
**Murphy's kidney punch:** a gentle fist to the renal angle to elicit tenderness in renal infection. Check for sacral oedema
**Rectal/pelvic examination:** enlarged prostate or a frozen pelvis as causes of obstruction

blocks.title: Scrotal mass
rows: Cystic, transilluminates, testis lies within it
Separate from the testis, does not transilluminate
Feels like a bag of worms
Varicocele (on the left, consider a left renal tumour or renal vein thrombosis)

blocks.title: Bedside urinalysis and microscopy
rows: Dysmorphic RBCs or red-cell casts (even one)
Dipstick blood but no RBCs on microscopy
Stones, interstitial nephritis, papillary necrosis, TB, interstitial cystitis
Favours pre-renal AKI over established ATN
Can be found in normal urine

blocks.text: On rectal examination, the **apparent size of the prostate** is a poor guide to whether it is causing obstruction.

blocks.note: Ballotting the kidney: one hand under the renal angle, the other on the anterior upper quadrant.
Murphy's kidney punch: a gentle fist strike to the renal angle.
Differential diagnosis of a scrotal mass by whether you can get above it, where it lies and whether it transilluminates.
Urine microscopy: normal-shaped RBCs (lower tract), dysmorphic RBCs (glomerular), hyaline casts (normal), red-cell cast (GN).

cards.back: < 100 mL urine per day (Talley uses < 50 mL/day; follow Davidson).

cards.front: What do months of polyuria and nocturia suggest in a patient with renal impairment?
cards.back: Long-standing CKD: failing tubules cannot concentrate urine, so volume rises.

cards.front: Blood only at the **start** of the stream, then clear urine: source?
cards.back: The urethra. Blood throughout = bladder or above; blood only at the end = prostate or bladder base.

cards.front: Dipstick strongly positive for blood but **no red cells** on microscopy?
cards.back: Haemoglobinuria (intravascular haemolysis) or myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis, brown urine).

cards.front: Visible haematuria, any age: what is the most likely cause and next step?
cards.back: Tumour. Refer to urology for ultrasound/CT and cystoscopy (after excluding UTI and menstruation).

cards.front: Loin pain after drinking a lot of beer (Dietl's crisis) suggests?

cards.back: Repeatedly passing small, painful volumes of bloody urine.

cards.front: Which single history feature most **lowers** the likelihood of UTI in a woman?
cards.back: Vaginal discharge (LR+ 0.3). Her own belief that she has a UTI raises it most (LR+ 4.0).

cards.front: Family history of deafness and kidney disease suggests?

cards.back: Both high (secondary: calcium low, phosphate high).

cards.front: Gum overgrowth in a renal transplant recipient?
cards.back: Calcineurin inhibitor (ciclosporin or tacrolimus); tremor is another clue to CNI toxicity.
Paired white transverse lines; hypoalbuminaemia, e.g. nephrotic syndrome.

cards.front: Examination of an AV fistula: what to feel and hear?
cards.back: A thrill over the anastomosis and a machinery murmur. Also check skin and look for aneurysms.

cards.front: Where do you listen for a renal bruit?
cards.back: About 2 cm either side of the midline above the umbilicus, then both flanks.

cards.front: White-cell casts in the urine suggest?

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
questions.theme: Urinary symptoms and urine volume terms

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with bilateral ureteric obstruction from retroperitoneal fibrosis has a urinary catheter. Over the last 24 hours it has drained 80 mL. Use Davidson’s definitions.
items.explanation: Davidson defines anuria as < 100 mL/day, so 80 mL/day is anuria. Talley’s cut-off is < 50 mL/day, which would call this oliguria; the exam follows Davidson. Bilateral ureteric obstruction is a classic cause of anuria.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman who has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for 10 years drinks water all day and measures her urine at 5 litres in 24 hours.
items.explanation: More than 3 L/24 hrs is polyuria. Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, one of the listed causes of polyuria.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man says that soon after he finishes passing urine and walks away from the toilet, he has to go back and pass a second amount.
items.explanation: Needing to void again shortly after finishing is pis-en-deux, a sign of incomplete emptying from bladder outflow obstruction, which is common in older men.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has noticed bright red blood at the very start of passing urine. The stream then clears for the rest of the void. He has no pain and no fever.
questions.leadIn: Where is the bleeding most likely to come from?
questions.explanation: The timing of blood in the stream localises the source. Blood at the start that then clears suggests the **urethra**. If the blood is mixed through the whole void, the source is the bladder or higher. Terminal blood (end of the stream only) suggests the prostate or bladder base.
whyNot: Bladder bleeding usually mixes through the whole stream.
Glomerular bleeding mixes throughout and often shows dysmorphic RBCs or casts.
Upper tract bleeding mixes throughout the urine.
Prostatic bleeding typically appears at the end of voiding, not the start.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man who smokes has passed red urine with small clots twice this week. He has no pain, no urinary symptoms and is not on anticoagulants. BP and eGFR are normal; urine culture is negative.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urology referral for imaging and cystoscopy
Reassure, as clots indicate a benign cause
questions.explanation: Davidson: visible haematuria is most often caused by **tumour**, so once UTI and menstruation are excluded the patient must go to **urology for ultrasound/CT and cystoscopy**. Clots also point to a non-glomerular (lower tract) source.
whyNot: Yearly observation is for non-visible haematuria in younger patients with normal BP, eGFR and ACR.
Nephrology and biopsy are for suspected glomerular disease (abnormal BP, eGFR, ACR or systemic features).
Quantifying protein does not exclude a urothelial tumour.
Clots point to a non-glomerular source; they do not make a tumour less likely.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
questions.theme: Causes of loin and lower abdominal pain
options: Acute urinary retention from prostatic enlargement

items.stem: A 32-year-old man has sudden, severe right loin pain that comes in waves and spreads into the right testis. He is restless and nauseated. Dipstick shows blood ++. There is marked loin tenderness.
items.explanation: Colicky loin pain radiating to the testis, haematuria and loin tenderness (LR+ 27.7) make renal colic from a ureteric stone most likely.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man has had several episodes of dull left flank ache. Each one starts a few hours after a night of heavy beer drinking and settles by the next day. He is otherwise well.
items.explanation: Loin pain brought on by a large fluid load (Dietl's crisis) suggests pelvi-ureteric junction obstruction: high urine flow distends the obstructed collecting system.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman had dysuria and frequency for 3 days and now has a temperature of 39.4 °C, rigors, vomiting and right back pain. A gentle fist strike to the right renal angle is painful.
items.explanation: Lower UTI symptoms progressing to high fever, vomiting, loin pain and renal angle tenderness indicate upper tract infection: acute pyelonephritis.

items.stem: An 81-year-old man is brought in confused and agitated. His wife says he has had a weak stream and hesitancy for years, and he has not passed urine since the morning. A dull, tender mass rises from the pelvis towards the umbilicus.
items.explanation: Two steps: confusion in an elderly man can be the only sign of retention; then the voiding LUTS history and a dull suprapubic mass point to acute retention from prostatic enlargement.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has microscopic haematuria on a sports medical. He has worn hearing aids since age 12. His maternal uncle started dialysis in his 30s.
questions.leadIn: Which diagnosis does the family history most suggest?
questions.explanation: Kidney disease running in a family together with **deafness** suggests **Alport syndrome** (hereditary nephritis with sensorineural hearing loss). On examination, look for hearing aids.
whyNot: PKD runs in families but causes flank pain, hypertension and big kidneys, not deafness.
IgA nephropathy causes recurrent haematuria but is not linked to deafness.
Reflux nephropathy is suggested by childhood bed-wetting and UTIs.
Analgesic nephropathy follows long-term compound analgesic use, not inheritance.

questions.stem: Routine bloods in a 58-year-old man show a creatinine of 410 µmol/L. Which single feature of his history best suggests that his kidney disease has been present for a long time?
questions.leadIn: Choose the most useful clue.
options: Getting up 3 times a night to pass large volumes of urine for 2 years
Passing less than 300 mL of urine a day for 3 days
Starting ibuprofen for back pain last week
Red-brown urine since a sore throat 2 weeks ago
questions.explanation: Long-standing **nocturia and polyuria** reflect failing tubular concentrating ability, which develops over time in CKD. Old test results (insurance or GP checks) also help date the disease.
whyNot: Oliguria is a pointer to a sudden kidney injury.
A recent NSAID suggests an acute insult, not chronicity.
Recent fluid loss suggests pre-renal AKI.
A recent nephritic illness points to an acute glomerulonephritis.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
questions.theme: Signs on renal examination and what they point to

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with a kidney transplant has thick, overgrown gums and a fine tremor of the outstretched hands.
items.explanation: Gingival hyperplasia and tremor are both clues to calcineurin inhibitor treatment (ciclosporin or tacrolimus).

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman on haemodialysis for 9 years has a grey-white band across both corneas in line with the opening of the eyelids. Her calcium and phosphate are both above the normal range, and she has a scar at the base of the neck.
items.explanation: Two steps: the corneal band is band keratopathy (calcium deposition); high calcium and phosphate in long-term dialysis fit tertiary hyperparathyroidism, and the neck scar suggests a parathyroidectomy.

items.stem: Three weeks after coronary angiography, a 68-year-old man with peripheral vascular disease has painful purple toes with small ulcers, a lace-like mottled rash on the legs and a rising creatinine.
items.explanation: Toe ulcers and livedo reticularis after an arterial procedure in an arteriopath point to atheroembolic disease.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with heavy proteinuria has two parallel white transverse lines across several fingernails.
items.explanation: Paired white transverse lines are Muehrcke's nails, seen in hypoalbuminaemia such as nephrotic syndrome.

questions.stem: You are examining the left loin of a patient with suspected hydronephrosis. You put one hand under the left renal angle and flick upwards, while your other hand rests on the left upper quadrant.
questions.leadIn: What is this technique called?
questions.explanation: **Ballotting** pushes the retroperitoneal kidney forwards so the anterior hand feels it rise and fall. It is the best way to feel a native kidney.
whyNot: The kidney punch is a gentle fist strike to the renal angle to elicit tenderness.
Auscultatory percussion is used to find the upper border of the bladder.
Shifting dullness is a test for ascites.
Transillumination is for scrotal swellings.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has hypertension that is poorly controlled on four drugs and a rising creatinine. Two months ago she had sudden pulmonary oedema with a normal echocardiogram. You hear a bruit with systolic and diastolic components 2 cm to the left of the midline above the umbilicus.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A **systolic-diastolic** bruit at the renal site in hard-to-control hypertension has LR+ > 40 for **renal artery stenosis**. "Flash" pulmonary oedema with renal impairment and hypertension adds to the likelihood.
whyNot: An aneurysm is felt as an expansile mass; it does not explain flash oedema and a renal-site diastolic bruit.
PKD causes palpable kidneys, not a renal-site diastolic bruit.
Splenic or aortic flow may cause a soft systolic bruit, not a systolic-diastolic one.
RCC presents with a loin mass and haematuria.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 21-year-old student has had four episodes of visible haematuria over 18 months, each starting a day or two into a cold or sore throat. Between episodes, dipstick shows a trace of blood. BP and creatinine are normal.
items.explanation: Repeated episodes over months, closely tied to upper respiratory infections, favour IgA nephropathy. A single nephritic illness with oedema, hypertension and oliguria would fit post-streptococcal GN instead.

items.stem: A 69-year-old ex-smoker has painless visible haematuria with clots. Urine culture is negative and renal function is normal.
items.explanation: Painless visible haematuria with clots in an older smoker: the commonest cause of visible haematuria is tumour, and clots point to a lower tract source.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man notices orange-red urine 3 weeks after starting treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis. Dipstick is negative for blood.
items.explanation: Red urine with a negative dipstick is not haematuria. Rifampicin, part of TB treatment, colours the urine.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman lay on her kitchen floor for 2 days after a fall before a neighbour came. Her urine is dark brown. Dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red cells. Creatinine is rising.
items.explanation: Two steps: a positive dipstick with no RBCs means a haem pigment, not red cells. Brown urine after a long lie makes it myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis, which also causes ATN.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man has vomited for 4 days and passed only 250 mL of urine in 24 hours. Urine specific gravity is 1.030 with a bland sediment.
items.explanation: Two steps: oliguria means an acute insult; concentrated urine (SG > 1.020) shows the tubules are still conserving water, which favours pre-renal AKI over established ATN.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has fever, right loin pain and vomiting. Urine microscopy shows many white cells and white-cell casts.
items.explanation: White-cell casts form in the tubules and strongly suggest pyelonephritis rather than a lower UTI.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man who moved from a high-TB region has night sweats and weight loss. Repeated urine samples show white cells, but routine cultures are always sterile.
items.explanation: Sterile pyuria has a short list of causes (stones, interstitial nephritis, papillary necrosis, TB, interstitial cystitis); systemic symptoms and origin point to TB.

items.stem: A 17-year-old has 1+ protein on a dipstick taken in the afternoon at a school medical. A first-morning sample is negative, and BP and renal function are normal.
items.explanation: Protein only in upright samples and not in the first-morning sample is orthostatic proteinuria, which is benign. This is why an early-morning sample is used.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man on the ward has a catheter that has drained 70 mL in the last 24 hours. An F1 says he is "oliguric, because anuria needs less than 50 mL".
questions.leadIn: How should his urine output be classified using Davidson’s definitions?
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** recall Davidson: oliguria is < 400 mL/day and anuria < 100 mL/day. **Step 2:** 70 mL/day is below 100, so it is **anuria**. **Step 3:** the F1 is using Talley’s cut-off (< 50 mL/day); the exam follows Davidson. **Step 4:** anuria should trigger a short differential: complete obstruction (check the catheter, bladder and kidneys), bilateral loss of perfusion, or RPGN.
whyNot: Oliguria applies under Talley’s definition only; by Davidson’s, 70 mL/day is anuria.
Normal adult output is about 800–2500 mL/day.
Polyuria is more than 3 L/24 hrs.
Nocturia is waking at night to void; it says nothing about the total volume.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman is referred with a creatinine of 520 µmol/L found on routine bloods. You are trying to decide whether this is acute or chronic.
questions.leadIn: Which examination finding most favours chronic kidney disease?
options: Dry mouth with a postural drop
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** list the signs that favour chronic disease: small kidneys, renal bone disease, normocytic anaemia and **peripheral neuropathy**. **Step 2:** look at what each option tells you. Volume signs (overload or depletion) show current fluid status, not how long the disease has been present. **Step 3:** loin tenderness and a palpable bladder point to infection or obstruction, which can be acute. Neuropathy takes time to develop, so it is the best clue to chronicity.
whyNot: Fluid overload can occur in AKI or CKD; it shows volume status, not duration.
Depletion signs suggest a pre-renal (often acute) process.
Loin tenderness suggests colic or infection, usually acute.
A palpable bladder suggests outflow obstruction, which may be acute.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man has bilateral irregular masses in both flanks that you can ballot, and a smooth enlarged liver. His father died suddenly of a brain haemorrhage at 50.
questions.leadIn: Which bedside measurement matters most next?
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** bilateral ballotable kidneys plus an enlarged liver (cysts) and a family history of sudden intracranial bleeding suggest **adult polycystic kidney disease**. **Step 2:** recall the PKD checklist: BP, dipstick for blood and protein, anaemia or polycythaemia, liver/spleen cysts, family screening. **Step 3:** about 75% are hypertensive, and BP is the first item on the checklist, so **measure BP** first.
whyNot: Glucose matters in diabetic nephropathy, not this picture.
Peak flow plays no part in PKD assessment.
Fever would matter only if a cyst seemed infected (tender kidney).
BMI does not change the key PKD assessment.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
questions.theme: History clues to the cause of acute kidney injury
options: Bilateral ureteric obstruction from pelvic malignancy

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman on ramipril and furosemide has had diarrhoea for 4 days. Her mouth is dry and her BP falls on standing. Creatinine has doubled.
items.explanation: Fluid loss plus an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic, with dry mouth and a postural drop, is the classic pre-renal history.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man has 6 weeks of new, constant back pain with tenderness over several vertebrae, and is now in renal failure. He has no previous kidney disease and both kidneys are of normal size.
items.explanation: Two steps: new back pain with vertebral tenderness suggests bone disease, and back pain in someone with renal failure should always raise suspicion of a paraprotein; myeloma is a classic disease with renal involvement, so myeloma cast nephropathy is most likely.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has had months of bloody nasal crusting, then coughs up blood and develops a purpuric rash on his shins. He is now passing little urine, with red-cell casts on microscopy.
items.explanation: Nasal discharge, haemoptysis and purpura are systemic inflammatory clues; with red-cell casts and oliguria this is a rapidly progressive GN from small-vessel (ANCA) vasculitis.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman treated for cervical cancer 2 years ago now passes no urine at all. Ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis, and pelvic examination finds a hard, fixed pelvis.
items.explanation: Complete anuria with bilateral hydronephrosis and a frozen pelvis indicates post-renal failure from bilateral ureteric obstruction by pelvic malignancy.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
questions.theme: Abdominal findings in the renal examination

items.stem: A 42-year-old man with BP 172/104 has large, irregular, ballotable masses in both flanks and an enlarged liver. His mother had a subarachnoid haemorrhage.
items.explanation: Bilateral irregular kidneys, liver cysts, hypertension and a family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage point to ADPKD.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with a kidney transplant 3 months ago has a fever, a rising creatinine and new tenderness over a smooth mass beneath a curved scar in the right iliac fossa.
items.explanation: Transplanted kidneys sit superficially in the iliac fossa; new tenderness over the graft with a rising creatinine may mean rejection.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has visible haematuria, weight loss and a ballotable mass in the left loin. On standing you also feel a soft "bag of worms" in the left side of the scrotum.
items.explanation: Two steps: a unilateral ballotable loin mass with haematuria suggests a renal tumour; a left varicocele supports it, because a left varicocele is sometimes found with an underlying left renal tumour (or left renal vein thrombosis).

items.stem: A slim, healthy 24-year-old woman has a smooth, non-tender lower pole felt in the right upper quadrant on deep inspiration. Renal function and urinalysis are normal.
items.explanation: A normal right kidney is on the list of causes of a unilateral palpable kidney; normal function, normal urine and no symptoms fit this benign finding.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has 2 days of urinary frequency and a yellow, itchy vaginal discharge. She has no fever.
questions.leadIn: Which feature in her history most lowers the likelihood that she has a UTI?
questions.explanation: In Talley’s evidence table, **vaginal discharge** has LR+ 0.3 and LR− 3.1: it makes UTI less likely and points to an alternative diagnosis. The woman’s own belief that she has a UTI is the strongest positive clue (LR+ 4.0).
whyNot: Frequency slightly raises the probability of UTI (LR+ 1.8).
Dysuria slightly raises the probability (LR+ 1.5).
Haematuria raises it (LR+ 2.0).
Flank pain is close to neutral (LR+ 1.1).

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease on haemodialysis is admitted with pneumonia. A student plans to take blood from the large, buzzing vein in his left forearm because it is easy to see.
questions.leadIn: What is the best advice?
options: Do not use the fistula arm for blood sampling
Use the fistula, as it gives fast flow
Use the fistula only with a tourniquet
Use the fistula only if the thrill is weak
Use the fistula and then apply firm pressure for 10 minutes
questions.explanation: The vessel is an **AV fistula**: the thrill and machinery murmur confirm a working access. It is the patient’s **dialysis lifeline**, and damaging it can seriously set back his care, so it must **never** be used for blood sampling.
whyNot: Easy access is exactly why fistulas get damaged; it must not be used.
A tourniquet adds risk to the fistula and does not make sampling acceptable.
A weak thrill may mean stenosis or thrombosis, which needs assessment, not sampling.
Pressure afterwards does not prevent damage from the puncture itself.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has a painless left scrotal swelling. When he stands, you cannot feel the upper edge of the swelling at the neck of the scrotum.
items.explanation: If you cannot get above a scrotal mass, it must be coming down the inguinal canal: an inguinoscrotal hernia.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man has a smooth, fluctuant swelling that surrounds the right testis so the testis cannot be felt separately. It lights up when a torch is pressed against it.
items.explanation: Cystic, transilluminating and enclosing the testis: fluid in the tunica vaginalis, a hydrocele.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man has a hard, painless lump arising from the body of the left testis. You can get above it, and it stays dark on transillumination.
items.explanation: A solid mass that is part of the testis is a tumour until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man has had nocturia, a weak stream and terminal dribbling for years. Now he leaks small amounts of urine all day and night. His lower abdomen is tender, with a dull mass reaching halfway to the umbilicus.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of his incontinence?
questions.explanation: Voiding LUTS from prostatic obstruction, constant dribbling and a **palpable, dull bladder** mean the bladder is full and leaking: **overflow incontinence** from chronic retention. Frequent small voids or leaks with a palpable bladder should always prompt this thought.
whyNot: Stress leakage occurs with coughing, mainly in women after childbirth or menopause, and the bladder is not distended.
Urge incontinence comes with sudden urgency and does not cause a palpable bladder.
UTI causes storage symptoms; it does not explain a large dull bladder.
A vesico-urethral fistula follows obstructed labour, does not fit a man with prostatic symptoms, and does not distend the bladder.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has 3 weeks of swollen ankles and puffy eyelids when she wakes. Her urine looks frothy. Her fingernails show two parallel white transverse bands, and she has pitting oedema to the knees.
questions.leadIn: Which syndrome best explains these findings?
questions.explanation: Frothy urine (heavy proteinuria), **facial oedema on waking** and paired white nail bands (**Muehrcke’s nails**, from low albumin) point to **nephrotic syndrome**: proteinuria > 3.5 g/24 hrs, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema.
whyNot: Nephritic syndrome causes red or brown urine, hypertension and oliguria rather than frothy urine.
Stage 5 CKD gives uraemic signs and half-and-half nails, not this picture.
Arsenic causes a single white band (Mees' line), not paired lines, and no frothy urine.
Heart failure causes dependent oedema but not frothy urine or morning facial puffiness.

ospe.identify: Advanced CKD signs: yellow complexion, pallor, brown-line nails, scratch marks, bruising, pericardial rub, raised JVP; RRT clues: AV fistula, dialysis line, Tenckhoff catheter, transplant scar.
Mees' line: a single transverse white band across the nail (arsenic, CKD). Compare Muehrcke's nails: paired lines in hypoalbuminaemia.
Forearm arteriovenous fistula for haemodialysis access: a longitudinal swelling over which a continuous thrill is felt.
Ballotting the kidney: posterior hand flicks up under the renal angle; anterior hand feels the kidney rise and fall.
Murphy's kidney punch: a gentle fist to the renal angle to elicit tenderness in renal infection.
Urine microscopy: dysmorphic RBCs and red-cell casts mean glomerular bleeding; normal-shaped RBCs mean lower tract bleeding; hyaline casts can be normal.
Transillumination of a hydrocele: a cystic swelling around the testis lights up with a torch; a solid tumour stays dark.
